title: Machine Learning for Fraud Detection in Digital Banking: A Systematic Literature Review
authors: George, M. Z. H.; Alam, M. K.; Hasan, M. T.
venue: ASRC Procedia: Global Perspectives in Science and Scholarship
tldr: A systematic review of 118 studies finds that supervised learning dominates digital banking fraud detection, unsupervised anomaly detection addresses novel fraud patterns, and hybrid models combining both paradigms demonstrate superior adaptability.
problem_and_motivation: Fraud in digital banking is evolving rapidly with new tactics such as synthetic identity creation and real-time transaction manipulation. Existing reviews lack comprehensive cross-regional and cross-methodological comparisons covering deep learning, hybrid models, and interpretability frameworks. A systematic synthesis is needed to consolidate fragmented findings across supervised, unsupervised, and deep learning approaches.
approach: Conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines, screening and including 118 peer-reviewed studies and institutional reports.

Organized the synthesis thematically around fraud definitions, machine learning paradigms, deep learning architectures, data imbalance challenges, interpretability, cross-regional insights, and deployment in banking ecosystems.
Compared supervised, unsupervised, and hybrid fraud detection approaches across performance trade-offs.
Analyzed cross-regional differences in fraud detection adoption shaped by EU PSD2/GDPR, North American fintech partnerships, and emerging economy infrastructure.
Identified gaps in reproducibility, robustness under distributional shift, and integration with criminological and governance frameworks.
findings: Supervised learning methods including decision trees, logistic regression, and SVMs remain dominant due to interpretability and established performance.
Unsupervised anomaly detection approaches are increasingly adopted to address novel fraud patterns in highly imbalanced datasets.
Deep learning architectures particularly LSTM and CNNs have emerged as transformative for modeling sequential transaction data.
Hybrid models combining supervised, unsupervised, and deep learning strategies demonstrate superior adaptability and detection accuracy.
Cross-regional analysis shows EU emphasizes PSD2/GDPR compliance, North America leverages fintech partnerships, and emerging economies depend on infrastructure maturity.

definitions.definition: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, a structured methodology for conducting systematic reviews.
Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique that generates synthetic minority-class samples to address class imbalance.
SHapley Additive exPlanations, a game-theoretic framework for explaining individual ML model predictions.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, a technique that approximates complex models with interpretable local surrogates.
Precision-Recall Area Under the Curve, a metric preferred over ROC-AUC for imbalanced fraud detection tasks.
Revised Payment Services Directive, EU regulation mandating open banking and strong customer authentication.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This systematic literature review consolidates 118 studies on machine learning for digital banking fraud detection, providing the most comprehensive cross-regional and cross-methodological comparison available. It maps the evolution from rule-based systems to supervised, unsupervised, deep learning, and hybrid approaches while highlighting how regulatory environments in the EU, North America, and emerging economies shape methodological adoption. The review identifies critical gaps in reproducibility, interpretability, and theoretical integration with governance frameworks.
directly_justifies: Supervised learning methods remain dominant in fraud detection due to interpretability and established performance.
Hybrid models combining supervised, unsupervised, and deep learning strategies demonstrate superior adaptability.
PSD2/SCA, GDPR, and payment harmonization form a regime where fraud detection is inseparable from regulatory compliance.
limits: Scope limited to English-language publications, potentially missing relevant non-English studies.
Heterogeneity of included studies limits direct quantitative meta-analysis.
Rapid evolution of fraud tactics means findings may become outdated quickly.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All topic domains were systematically scanned. Domains 4.A and 4.B are highly relevant as the paper surveys the landscape of existing fraud detection systems and their limitations. Domain 8.A is highly relevant due to extensive coverage of unsupervised anomaly detection methods. Domain 8.B is medium relevance as the paper discusses algorithms but does not present original spending data analysis. Domains 1-3, 5-7, 9-14 were considered and rejected: the paper does not address Filipino demographics, budgeting, mobile design, privacy, engagement, savings, debt, or synthetic data generation.

limitations: English-only publication filter may exclude relevant research from non-English journals.
Heterogeneity of included studies prevents direct quantitative meta-analysis.
Rapidly evolving fraud tactics and ML methods mean the review may require frequent updating.
remember_this: Supervised learning dominates digital banking fraud detection for interpretability and performance.
Hybrid models combining supervised and unsupervised approaches outperform single-paradigm methods.
Regulatory environments shape how fraud detection is implemented across different regions.
PR-AUC is preferred over ROC-AUC for evaluating imbalanced fraud datasets.
Gaps remain in reproducibility, robustness, and interpretability of fraud detection systems.
